newsitem.title: USA: Walter, late of AT&T, shied from public eye.
newsitem.headline: Walter, late of AT&T, shied from public eye.

text.p: Behind John Walter's sudden departure Wednesday as president and chief operating officer at AT&T Corp -- and the heir apparent to Chief Executive Robert Allen -- may have been a reluctance to face the public scrutiny that comes with heading the nation's largest phone company.

Analysts said Walter may have been unprepared for the harsh public review of career, capabilities and personality that he faced immediately after being named as the future head of the nation's largest long-distance company.
Walter joined AT&T in November after a closely watched search for a new executive that could one day fill the shoes of Allen, who is also AT&T's chairman.
Several analysts said that after nearly nine months on the job, little more was known about Walter outside the company than what had been published at the time of his arrival.
His prior career at directory publisher R.R. Donnelley & Sons & Co. and his lack of telecommunications industry experience met with bruising critiques from the day he was hired.

"For someone who was taking the reigns at AT&T, he needed to be front and center," industry analyst Jeffrey Kagan said of Walter's retreat from the limelight. Kagan runs Kagan Telecom Associates in Atlanta.

Walter was in an unenviable position at AT&T, the once-undisputed giant of the U.S. phone industry, having to contend with frequent criticism of a company which in recent years has been facing rising competition in its core long-distance markets and the strategic need to expand into new businesses like local services, cellular and the Internet.

The plan was for Walter to take over as chief executive in January 1998, subject to the approval of AT&T's board. It was the board's decision to delay his elevation beyond the January date that led Walter to resign, AT&T said.

Upon his arrival last November, Walter was given key operating responsibilities as an on-the-job tutorial designed to give him wider experience of the company before he was elevated to chief executive.
He focused his attentions on meeting customers and employees but shied from the limelight, sources familiar with his short tenure at AT&T said.
Earlier this year, Several analysts began publicly asking, "Where is John Walter?"

He was given a promiment role at a major meeting with Wall Street analysts in March -- during which AT&T had warned that earnings would be depressed for several years due to heavy investments in new businesses like local service and cellular.
But since then, he had once again taken a back seat to Allen, the voluable showman who has headed AT&T since 1988.

At AT&T's annual meeting in May, Walter met with widespread boos from an audience of restive shareholders after he jokingly dismissed an audience question about the hundreds of thousands of moving expenses he had billed the company in relocating to New Jersey from his former home in Illinois.
Over time, Walter lost the confidence of those who had hired him that he had the leadership qualities to take on the top job at AT&T -- the board of directors, including Allen.

In a conference call Wednesday, board member Walter Elisha said Allen had begun expressing his reservations about Walter as early as April. On Tuesday night, the eight independent directors on AT&T's board voted to delay Walter's accession.

Walter responded by resigning from his posts at AT&T. Under terms of his employment contract with AT&T, he will receive separation payments of $3.8 million, in addition to a compenation package of $22 million AT&T provided him to replace salary, pension and bonuses he forfeited when he left R.R. Donnelley to join AT&T.
